title: The Numbers Behind The Knicks Title Run Are Absurd — And Everyone Is Coming Back
thumb_prompt: a dark Madison Square Garden court seen from above with faint statistical lines and glowing numbers projected onto the hardwood, single spotlight, haze
thumb_subject: a point guard in a blue and orange jersey standing alone at centre court

paragraphs.text: Fresh off their first title in more than forty years, the New York Knicks are the team most likely to dominate this entire league next season. And when you actually sit down with the numbers behind this roster, the picture gets even clearer. So let us go through them, one man at a time.
We start with the reigning Finals MVP, Jalen Brunson. He enters next season carrying a resume not many players in this league can match.

He is coming off a 2026 regular season where he played 74 games and started every single one of them. He averaged 26 points, 6.8 assists and 3.3 rebounds a night, all while logging 35 minutes a game. That is a massive workload for any guard in this league.

Now here is something wild. His scoring average was identical in back to back seasons. In 2024-25 he also averaged 26 points a game. But dig into the shooting numbers and things shifted. His field goal percentage dropped from 48.8 percent to 46.7 percent. His three point percentage dropped from 38.3 percent to 36.9 percent. But his free throw percentage actually climbed, from 82.1 percent up to 84.1 percent.

His three point attempts kept climbing throughout his Knicks years. Back in 2022-23 he was only taking 4.7 threes a game. That jumped to 6.8 the next year, dipped slightly to 6.1, and then shot up to 7.1 attempts per game this past season. The highest of his entire Knicks career.

Once the playoffs started, everything changed for Brunson. He played all 19 playoff games and dropped 539 total points, which led every single player in the entire postseason. Victor Wembanyama was second with 524. His team went sixteen and three across the whole run.

Here is a stat that puts his postseason scoring into perspective. His career regular season scoring average sits at 19.2 points per game. His career playoff scoring average is 25.7 points per game. That is a jump of 6.5 points, and that jump is the largest playoff scoring increase in league history among players with at least 500 regular season games and 50 playoff appearances.

In the clutch, his numbers get even more ridiculous. Since the 2023 postseason he has racked up 144 clutch playoff points. No other player in that stretch had more than 85. He also piled up 364 fourth quarter playoff points over that same span, with the next closest player, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, sitting at 292.

Then came the Finals, and Brunson somehow elevated even further. He averaged 32.6 points, 4.2 rebounds and 4.6 assists across five games against the Spurs. His clutch scoring in that series hit 22 points, the most by any player in a Finals series over the previous fifteen years. He walked away with Finals MVP honors.

Now let us talk about what is actually settled heading into next season. Brunson is under contract for roughly 37.7 million dollars. That represents about 22.7 percent of the league salary cap, which sits at just under 165 million dollars.

He is not testing free agency anytime soon either, since he is locked in through the 2028-29 season, with that final year being a player option. Age wise, Brunson turns thirty on August thirty first, 2026. So essentially his entire upcoming season will be played as a thirty year old, heading into his ninth year in the league.
card_lines: Final year is a player option

paragraphs.text: On the health side there is one major factor to track. Brunson had surgery on July seventh, 2026 to repair a tendon issue in his left wrist and forearm. The reported recovery window was six to eight weeks, and reports suggested he could be fully healed by training camp in September. But that is a projection, not a guarantee, so it is worth watching closely as the season approaches.

As for the roster around him, the core group is staying intact. Karl-Anthony Towns, who averaged 20.1 points and 11.9 rebounds. Mikal Bridges, who averaged 14.4 points while shooting 49 percent from the field and 37.1 percent from three. OG Anunoby, who posted 16.7 points a night. And Josh Hart, who chipped in 12 points, 7.4 rebounds and 4.8 assists a game.

So when you add it all up, Brunson is stepping into next season as a thirty year old reigning Finals MVP, fresh off a 539 point playoff run, a 32.6 point Finals average, and a fully returning championship core around him. The numbers alone tell the story of a player operating at the absolute peak of his career.
By the way, if you enjoy these deep dives, I will be posting every day. I genuinely appreciate it if you could subscribe. Thanks. Anyway, up next.
card_lines: Subscribe if this is your thing

paragraphs.text: Karl-Anthony Towns steps into next season with a stat sheet that tells a totally different story than most people realize. In 2025-26 he played 75 games, starting every single one, and put up 20.1 points, 11.9 rebounds and 3 assists a night, all in 31 minutes of action.

Here is where it gets interesting though. That 20.1 scoring average was actually a drop from his first year in New York. In 2024-25 he averaged 25.2 points, 13.2 rebounds and 3.2 assists. So his scoring fell by 5.1 points per game, and his rebounding dropped by 1.3 boards a night.

His shooting percentages shifted too. Field goal percentage went from 52.6 percent down to 50.1 percent. His three point percentage dropped from 42 percent all the way to 36.8 percent. But his free throw shooting actually climbed, jumping from 82.9 percent up to 85.8 percent.

Now here is the number that really stands out. His career three point percentage sits at 39.7 percent. So even with the dip, he is still knocking down shots at a rate that forces defenses to respect him beyond the arc. He was attempting around 4.1 threes a game and making about 1.5 of them a night.

Once the playoffs hit, Towns transformed into something totally different. He played all 19 playoff games, and his assist numbers jumped from 3 per game in the regular season up to roughly 4.9 assists per game in the postseason. That is a jump of nearly two assists a night. He finished with 94 total assists and 50 turnovers, an assist to turnover ratio of about 1.9 to one.

Break it down by series and it gets even wilder. Against Atlanta in the first round he averaged six assists per game over six games. Against Philadelphia in the second round that number jumped to 7.5 assists per game across four games, with only nine total turnovers in the entire series. His assist to turnover ratio in that stretch was 3.3 to one, which is an absurd number for a seven footer.

On April thirtieth, 2026 against Atlanta, Towns recorded 12 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists, giving him a playoff triple double. That made him just the third player in franchise history to pull that off, joining Walt Frazier and Josh Hart.

His passing was not just going to one guy either. Over the playoffs he dished out 21 assists to Brunson, 19 to Josh Hart, 18 to OG Anunoby, 15 to Mikal Bridges, eight to Jordan Clarkson, six to Jose Alvarado, four to Miles McBride, two to Landry Shamet and one to Mitchell Robinson.

His plus minus during the run was staggering too. Reports have him at plus 262 for the entire postseason, which would top names like Stephen Curry at plus 245 in 2017 and Draymond Green at plus 227 that same year. During the four game sweep of Cleveland in the Eastern Conference Finals he posted a plus 79, matching Kevin Durant's plus 79 from the 2017 Conference Finals.

Towns played all 19 playoff games for around 578 total minutes, averaging about 30.4 minutes a game. New York went sixteen and three across the whole postseason, and their point differential of plus 283 was the highest in NBA postseason history.

Let us talk contract numbers now. Towns is set to make roughly 57.8 million dollars in the upcoming season. That makes him the highest paid player on the entire Knicks roster, ahead of OG Anunoby at 42.5 million, Jalen Brunson at 37.7 million, Mikal Bridges at 33.5 million and Josh Hart at 20.9 million.
His salary alone equals about 34.6 percent of the entire salary cap. And his contract does not stop there either. He has roughly 61.2 million dollars locked in for the following season as well.

Age wise, Towns turns thirty one during the upcoming season, and he is heading into his twelfth year in the league. He was the number one overall pick back in 2015 out of Kentucky, and he is now a six time All-Star, a three time All-NBA selection, and the 2015-16 Rookie of the Year.

One roster change worth tracking is that Mitchell Robinson is no longer with the team, which puts even more importance on Towns holding down the center spot. New York did bring in Andre Drummond as depth behind him though, so it is not like the cupboard is completely empty at that position.

His career averages tell the bigger picture too. 22.8 points, 11.1 rebounds and 3.1 assists a game, shooting 52.2 percent from the field, 39.7 percent from three and 84 percent from the line. Heading into next season he brings elite rebounding, efficient shooting for his size, and a passing role that expanded in a massive way during the championship run.
And we cannot talk about the Knicks success without covering OG Anunoby, who heads into next season carrying two championship rings. The numbers behind his rise are honestly kind of wild.

Let us start with his regular season. He played 67 games, starting every one of them, averaging 16.7 points, 5.2 rebounds, 2.2 assists, 1.6 steals and 0.7 blocks a night. He shot 48.4 percent from the field, 38.6 percent from three and 82.8 percent from the free throw line.

That scoring number is a big jump from his career average, which sits at 13.3 points per game. So he was scoring 3.4 points above his career mark, and he did it while only taking 12 field goal attempts a game. He was not jacking up shots to get there either, attempting about 6.1 threes and 3.3 free throws per game.

His efficiency backs this up too. His effective field goal percentage was 58.1 percent, well above his career mark of 56.3 percent. His true shooting percentage sat at 62 percent for the regular season. And his free throw shooting jumped from a career mark of 77.4 percent up to 82.8 percent.

Then the playoffs happened, and Anunoby basically became a different player statistically. Over 17 playoff games he averaged 20.1 points, 6.3 rebounds, 1.6 assists, 1.5 steals and 1.1 blocks a night. His shooting splits during that stretch were absurd. 56.1 percent from the field, 48.9 percent from three, and 85.4 percent from the line, giving him a true shooting percentage of 72.1 percent.

That is a jump of 3.4 points per game in scoring from the regular season to the playoffs, and a 10.3 percentage point jump in his three point shooting. His true shooting number climbed by over ten percentage points too. And here is the kicker. His turnovers actually dropped from 1.8 per game in the regular season down to 0.6 per game in the playoffs. Only ten total turnovers across all 17 games.

He did miss two playoff games with a hamstring strain suffered late in game two against Philadelphia, sitting out games three and four of that series. At the time of the injury he was averaging 21.4 points per game in the postseason on 61.9 percent shooting from the field and 53.8 percent from three. He returned in time for game one of the Eastern Conference Finals and never missed another game.

His individual playoff scoring games were massive too. He dropped 29 points against Atlanta, 24 against Philadelphia before the injury, 21 against Cleveland, 28 in Finals game three, and 33 in Finals game four. That 33 point outburst came on ten of fifteen shooting, including seven of nine from three. That is 77.8 percent from deep in that game alone.

sections.heading: STILL ONE OF THE BEST DEFENDERS ALIVE

paragraphs.text: Defensively, Anunoby remains one of the best two way players in the league. He earned a spot on the 2025-26 All-Defensive Second Team, his second career All-Defensive selection, and he finished tenth in Defensive Player of the Year voting. Across the regular season he racked up 104 steals and 48 blocks over 67 games.

His playoff defensive matchups shot just 42.8 percent against him. And during fourth quarters specifically, opponents shot just 34.8 percent when he was the primary defender. His win shares number for the 2026 playoffs was 3.8, which led the entire postseason field.
card_lines: Best win shares in the playoffs

paragraphs.text: According to Basketball Reference, his overall plus minus for the regular season was plus 407, and his playoff plus minus came in at plus 163 across 17 games.

Now let us talk contract. Anunoby is set to earn 42.5 million dollars this season, making him the second highest paid player on the Knicks behind Towns. His deal runs through the 2028-29 season, with roughly 45.4 million coming the year after this one and 48.4 million in the final year. That salary represents about 25.6 percent of this season's cap.

Age wise, Anunoby is 29 years old, born July seventeenth, 1997, making this his tenth season in the league. He was drafted twenty third overall back in 2017 out of Indiana, spending seven seasons in Toronto before landing in New York. His career numbers jumped significantly after the move, going from 11.8 points per game in Toronto up to 16.9 points per game as a Knick.

He is now a two time NBA champion, picking up his first ring with Toronto back in 2019, though he missed that playoff run due to an emergency appendectomy. This most recent title with New York was a completely different story, since he played a massive role throughout the entire postseason.

sections.heading: AND THEN THERE IS JOSH HART

paragraphs.text: One other key part of their win was Josh Hart, and he too enters next season as an NBA champion. His stat line tells one of the most unusual stories on the entire Knicks roster.

He played 66 games last season, starting 52 of them, and averaged 12 points, 7.4 rebounds, 4.8 assists and 1.1 steals a night in just over 30 minutes of action. He shot 50.8 percent from the field, 41.3 percent from three and 72 percent from the free throw line, giving him a true shooting percentage of 61.2 percent.

Let us talk about that rebounding number first, because it is honestly ridiculous. Hart stands at six foot five and 215 pounds, yet he pulled down 7.4 boards a game. That included 1.4 offensive rebounds and six defensive rebounds a night. League wide, that rebounding average ranked twenty seventh in the entire NBA, and his 4.8 assists per game ranked thirty seventh. For a guy his size, those numbers put him in company with much bigger players.

Across the whole regular season Hart racked up 792 points, 486 rebounds, 317 assists, 75 steals and 17 blocks. He also finished with a plus 210 plus minus and 6.1 win shares, both well above his career average. His player efficiency rating came in at 15.7, compared to his career mark of 13.5.

Now here is where things get really interesting. His three point shooting jumped to 41.3 percent, a career best by a wide margin, since his career average sits at 35 percent. That is a 6.3 percentage point jump. And he was not chucking up threes to get there either, attempting only 3.7 a game. His field goal percentage of 50.8 percent was also well above his career average of 47.5 percent.

Then the playoffs rolled around and Hart's role shifted in a fascinating way. He played all 19 playoff games. His scoring actually dropped to 10.4 points a game, but his rebounding jumped up to 8.9 boards a night. His assists stayed steady at 4.6 per game, and his steals climbed from 1.1 up to 1.7.

His shooting efficiency did take a hit. His field goal percentage dropped to 43.1 percent and his three point shooting fell to 32.6 percent, bringing his true shooting down to 52.5 percent. But here is the wild part. His individual defensive rating improved from 111.6 in the regular season all the way down to 101.1 in the playoffs. A difference of 10.5 points per 100 possessions. And his plus minus for the postseason was an absurd plus 201 across those 19 games.

The Finals were where his rebounding really took off. Across five games against San Antonio, Hart averaged 7.6 points, 9.8 rebounds and 4.6 assists. In game one alone he grabbed 15 rebounds to go with six assists, four steals and one block, all while scoring just three points.

Then in game two he scored zero points but still pulled down six rebounds with four assists, one steal and one block. And in the championship clinching game five he finished with 13 points and 11 rebounds, including three offensive boards.

Hart also played through multiple injuries during the season. He dealt with a left thumb sprain during the Eastern Conference semi-finals against Philadelphia, with X-rays confirming there was no fracture. He also carried over a right ring finger issue from a procedure back in July of 2025, choosing to play through it with a splint rather than have surgery that would keep him off the court.

sections.heading: THE HISTORY HART IS ALREADY IN

paragraphs.text: Let us get into the history now, because this part is wild too. Hart set the Knicks single season franchise record for triple doubles in the 2024-25 season with nine, breaking a record that had stood since Walt Frazier set it at eight back in 1968-69. That record stood for fifty six years before Hart broke it.
He also had six triple doubles the year before that, giving him fifteen total across two seasons, tying him with LeBron James over that same stretch.

His college career adds another layer here too. Hart played at Villanova, winning the 2016 National Championship alongside current teammate Jalen Brunson. That connection goes all the way back to college, and now they are NBA champions together in New York.

Contract wise, Hart is set to earn roughly 20.9 million dollars this season, with 22.4 million coming the year after. That makes him the lowest paid member of the Knicks five man championship core, sitting well below Towns at 57.8 million, Anunoby at 42.5, Brunson at 37.7 and Bridges at 33.5.
Age wise, Hart is 31 years old, born March sixth, 1995, and he is entering his tenth season in the league after being drafted thirtieth overall back in 2017.

So when you put it all together, Hart brings a statistical profile that does not rely on scoring to make an impact. His rebounding climbed at every level of competition, going from 7.4 in the regular season up to 8.9 in the playoffs and then 9.8 in the Finals. Combine that with career best shooting, a franchise triple double record and steady playmaking, and you have a player whose value shows up in categories way beyond the box score.

Let us now shift our focus towards Mikal Bridges, who heads into next season as an NBA champion for the very first time. And his numbers tell the story of a player who completely reshaped his role to fit a title winning team.

He played all 82 games last season, starting every single one, averaging 32.8 minutes a night. His stat line came out to 14.4 points, 3.8 rebounds, 3.7 assists, 1.3 steals and 0.8 blocks a game. He shot 49 percent from the field, 37.1 percent from three and 82.7 percent from the free throw line.

Now here is something wild about his durability. Bridges extended his consecutive game streak to 638 straight games last season, the longest active streak in the entire NBA. That streak stretches all the way back to his rookie year, spanning three different franchises. In one especially strange stretch back in 2022-23 he actually played 83 total games across two teams after being traded mid-season. 56 with Phoenix and 27 with Brooklyn.

His scoring did drop compared to his first season in New York. He averaged 17.6 points per game in his first Knicks season, and that fell to 14.4 this past year. But here is the twist. His efficiency actually went up. His field goal percentage climbed from 46.3 percent to 49 percent, while his usage rate dropped from 18.6 percent down to 15.4 percent. He was taking on a smaller offensive role while shooting the ball better than ever.

Nearly half of his shot attempts came from three point range, with 43.6 percent of his field goals being threes. On catch and shoot threes specifically he knocked down 37.5 percent. And he was incredibly efficient inside ten feet, shooting 68.3 percent from that range.

Then the playoffs hit and Bridges elevated his game in a massive way. Across all 19 playoff games, all of which he started, he averaged 13.5 points, 3.2 rebounds, 2.7 assists, one steal and 0.3 blocks in 32 minutes a night. His shooting jumped to 55.9 percent from the field and 36.5 percent from three. His free throw shooting rose to an incredible 92 percent, and his true shooting for the playoffs hit 64.3 percent.

His advanced numbers during that run were outstanding too. His offensive rating sat at 119.5, his defensive rating at 103.8, giving him a net rating of plus 15.7. His assist to turnover ratio was 3.06, and he finished the playoffs at plus 195 across those 19 games.

He had some huge individual performances too. He dropped 24 points on ten of twelve shooting against Atlanta. He scored 22 against Cleveland while adding three steals and two blocks. And in the Finals he had a game with 20 points, six rebounds and six assists on eight of thirteen shooting and four of six from three.

Speaking of the Finals, Bridges averaged 10.4 points, 3.6 rebounds and 3.4 assists across the five games against San Antonio, shooting 46.5 percent from the field and 42.1 percent from three. Both numbers topped his regular season marks. And in the championship clinching game five he closed things out with 14 points, four assists and a block in nearly 39 minutes.

Let us talk contract now. Bridges signed a four year, 150 million dollar extension with New York back on August first, 2025, before any of this championship run even happened. His salary for this upcoming season sits at roughly 33.5 million dollars. That climbs to 36.2 million the year after, then 38.8 million, with a player option worth 41.5 million in the final season.

Age wise, Bridges is currently 29 years old, born August thirtieth, 1996, meaning he turns thirty right around the start of next season. He was drafted tenth overall back in 2018 by Philadelphia before being traded to Phoenix on draft night. New York acquired him from Brooklyn in July of 2024, giving up five future first round picks, a pick swap and a future second rounder to get him.

His career path has taken him through very different offensive roles. In Phoenix he was mostly a complementary two way piece. During his stint in Brooklyn his usage rate spiked to nearly 30 percent and he averaged over 20 points a game. But in New York his usage dropped back down to around 15 percent, and his shooting efficiency reached the best levels of his career.

He also has one previous Finals appearance, back in 2021 with Phoenix, though that team came up short against Milwaukee. This time around, five years later, he finally got the ring. So he enters next season as a 29 year old champion who just posted the most efficient stretch of basketball in his career, by scoring less and shooting better than ever before.
And we cannot forget about Jose Alvarado, who enters next season with a brand new contract and a championship ring. His path to get there is one of the more interesting stories on this roster.

Let us start with the contract, because it is a big deal. Alvarado declined his 4.5 million dollar player option and instead signed a new three year deal worth more than 14 million with the Knicks, made official on July sixth, 2026. That means there is zero uncertainty here. He is locked in with New York beyond this upcoming season.

Age wise, Alvarado is 28 years old, born April twelfth, 1998, heading into his sixth NBA season. He stands at six feet tall and 179 pounds, making him one of the smaller guards in the league. He went undrafted back in 2021 out of Georgia Tech, and his career path took him from New Orleans all the way to New York.

The Knicks acquired him mid-season at the February trade deadline in 2026, sending Dalen Terry, two second round picks and cash to New Orleans in return. So his time in New York last season was not even a full season. It was a partial sample after the trade.
card_lines: Half a season in New York

paragraphs.text: Across both stops he appeared in 69 games, averaging 7.4 points, 2.5 rebounds, 3.4 assists and one steal a night, shooting 41.6 percent from the field, 35.2 percent from three and 76.1 percent from the line. Once he landed with the Knicks specifically, his role became clear. Over 28 regular season games he averaged 16.9 minutes, 6.6 points, 3.8 assists and one steal, starting just three of them.

sections.heading: THE NIGHT ALVARADO CHANGED A FINAL

paragraphs.text: Then the playoffs hit and his role shrunk even further in terms of minutes. Across all 18 playoff games he averaged just 9.4 minutes a night, putting up 4.2 points, 1.4 rebounds, 1.2 assists and 0.6 steals, shooting 43.3 percent from the field and 35.3 percent from three. He did not start a single playoff game.

But here is where things get interesting. Before the playoffs even started, reports indicated Mike Brown's probable nine man playoff rotation did not even include Alvarado. He was on the outside looking in, based on that initial plan. Yet by the time the Finals rolled around, he became one of the most memorable role players of the entire championship run.

That moment came in game four of the NBA Finals. San Antonio built a 29 point lead over New York. The Knicks stormed back to win 107 to 106, and Alvarado was a massive part of it. He played nine minutes and forty seconds in the fourth quarter alone, scoring eight points, dishing three assists and grabbing two rebounds. He went three for three from three point range during that stretch.

The Knicks outscored San Antonio by 17 points during his fourth quarter minutes on the floor. Mike Brown specifically credited him after the game for changing things. That stint also included him playing alongside Jalen Brunson, who went on to win Finals MVP. Brown made the choice to use Alvarado in that crunch time situation instead of Mikal Bridges, giving the Knicks another ball handler and shooter next to their primary offensive engine.

His shooting numbers tell a pretty consistent story across his career too. His career three point percentage sits at 34.9 percent. His 2025-26 mark was 35.2 percent, and his playoff percentage with the Knicks came in at 35.3 percent. All three land right around the same mid thirties range.

One of the wildest individual games of his season came on February eleventh, 2026 against Philadelphia, when he dropped 26 points off the bench, making eight three pointers and racking up five steals. That performance made him the first player in Knicks history to come off the bench and put up at least 25 points, five steals and five made threes in the same game.

His defensive reputation is built around ball pressure, quickness and disruption, which earned him the nickname Grand Theft Alvarado. On a roster full of expensive stars, he is the cheapest thing on it, and one of the reasons the season ended the way it did.

sections.heading: WHAT ALL OF THIS ADDS UP TO

paragraphs.text: So put it all together. A thirty year old Finals MVP at the peak of his career. A seven footer who turned into a playmaker at exactly the right moment. A two way wing who shot 48.9 percent from three in the postseason and gave up only ten turnovers in 17 games. And an undersized champion who rebounds like a forward and passes like a guard.

That is the group New York is bringing back. Not a team that got hot for six weeks, but a roster whose numbers held up under the brightest lights in the sport. Which is exactly why everyone else in this league spent the summer trying to figure out how to beat them. Tell me in the comments who you think matches up with this team, because right now I am struggling to find one.
